segments.caption: A vertical log hive, inoculated with propolis and beeswax and mounted 10 feet high in a tree with three entrance holes and an observation port, is shown as a swarm of bees moves in on April 4, 2013, settling into its new home.

The video shows a close-up of a large tree trunk with a noticeable, roughly circular opening cut into it, revealing the lighter-colored wood inside. A hand enters the frame, pointing to the opening while a rope is looped around its edge. Text on screen identifies this as the “First opening,” taken six days after an event referred to as “birth,” dated April 10, 2013. The surrounding scene is a forest with dense green foliage and branches

A person carefully opens a wooden panel secured to a tree trunk with rope, revealing a small, dark hole inside the wood. The camera then zooms in to show the interior of the tree, where several small, dark holes are visible, suggesting the presence of a colony of insects or a nesting animal. The scene is set outdoors in a wooded area.

A close-up view reveals a dense cluster of bees actively swarming and moving within a wooden cavity, with the scene shifting to show the bees covering a dark, textured surface, indicating a hive or nest being explored or harvested.

A close-up view shows a dense cluster of dark, wriggling insect larvae, likely from a bee or wasp nest, being examined. The scene then shifts to an outdoor setting where a hand opens a wooden cavity in a tree trunk, revealing a small, dark opening inside. Text on screen indicates this is the “Second Opening,” 17 days after the nest’s “birth” on April 21, 2013, suggesting the footage documents the

The frames show a close-up view inside a wooden structure, revealing a dense cluster of bees actively building and tending to their honeycomb, which is partially covered in a white, waxy substance, indicating a thriving and active hive.

A bee swarm is shown in close-up, densely packed and actively moving, before the camera pans to reveal its origin: a natural hole in a tree trunk. Text indicates this is the “Third Opening,” 37 days after the swarm’s “birth” on May 11, 2013. The final shot shows the tree with a circular cut and a rope tied across it, suggesting human intervention to manage or relocate the hive.
A person pulls a rope taut across a freshly cut tree hole, revealing a dense swarm of bees packed tightly inside the cavity, indicating the discovery of a hidden beehive.

A large swarm of bees, covered in white powder, clings to the inside of a tree cavity, while a human hand ties a rope around the tree trunk, marking the fourth opening eleven weeks after the swarm’s “birth” on June 22, 2013.

A person's hand is shown interacting with a large, circular opening cut into the trunk of a tree, which appears to be a treehouse or tree fort. The hand, wearing a ring, repeatedly touches and points to the smooth, light-colored inner wood of the opening, while a patterned rope is tied around the tree trunk nearby. Text overlaid on the first frame indicates this is the "Forth opening," 11 weeks after "birth," dated June 2
A person carefully removes a section of bark from a tree trunk, revealing a large, active bee hive teeming with bees inside the hollow cavity.

A beekeeper carefully removes a large, hollowed-out section of a tree trunk, revealing a dense swarm of bees clustered inside and on the exposed wood, then lifts the entire section to inspect the colony before setting it aside.

The video opens on a large, rugged tree trunk, secured with ropes, setting the scene for an apiary operation. The camera then moves to reveal a hollowed-out cavity within the tree, which serves as a natural beehive. Inside, a dense swarm of bees is actively tending to their honeycomb structures, which are visible with their characteristic hexagonal cells. A dense swarm of bees actively moves across and around honeycomb frames inside a wooden hive, showcasing the colony’s bustling, cooperative activity within its natural structure.
A person gently inspects a live honeycomb, their hand brushing over the dense cluster of bees swarming across the hexagonal wax cells within a wooden hive.

A close-up view of a bustling beehive, showing bees actively moving over honeycomb cells, before transitioning to a dark, blurry interior shot, then fading to a textured, aged paper background, and finally to black.
